opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that the playbook has changed underneath people, and the instincts that served them really well in one era can actively mislead them in this one.

If you built your career scaling, say, a SaaS company or a mobile-era consumer business, you learned a set of patterns that worked. You knew roughly how long it took to build a feature, how to staff a team, how to run a planning cycle, how much engineering effort translated into how much product. Those were hard-won lessons, and they were correct for that world. But AI changes some of the basic economics. When a small team with good AI coding assistants can prototype something in a day that used to take a month, the bottleneck shifts. It's no longer "can we build it?" Increasingly it's "what should we build?" and "how fast can we get feedback from users?" Product management, decision-making speed, and judgment about what to try become the constraint, and leaders who are still optimizing for engineering throughput can end up optimizing the wrong thing.

A second piece is that the technology is moving so fast that experience can have a shorter half-life. Something that was true about model capabilities eighteen months ago may simply not be true today. Leaders who succeeded before often have strong, confident mental models, and that confidence is an asset until the ground shifts. Then it becomes a liability if they're not hands-on enough to notice. I find the leaders who do well in AI companies tend to stay close to the technology. They actually play with the models, they try the tools themselves, they build a little. That gives them an intuition for what's now easy, what's still hard, and what's just become possible, which you really can't get from reading slide decks.

And third, there's the question of process and risk tolerance. Many larger-company practices exist to reduce the risk of expensive mistakes, so you get lots of reviews, long planning horizons, and careful sign-offs. When building was expensive, that made sense. But when experimentation is cheap, those processes can slow you down far more than they protect you. In AI, the winning move is often to run many fast, low-cost experiments, keep the ones that work, and be responsible about the ones that touch real users or real safety concerns. Some experienced leaders bring over the heavyweight process wholesale, and it suffocates the speed that's actually the company's biggest advantage.

None of this means experience doesn't matter. Things like hiring great people, building culture, understanding customers, and go-to-market are still deeply important. But the leaders who thrive are the ones who can hold onto those fundamentals while being genuinely humble and curious about what's changed, and willing to relearn parts of the job from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says AI makes experimentation cheap and that heavyweight reviews and long planning horizons can suffocate the speed AI companies need, describing a mismatch with leaders’ accustomed pace.

r002.rationale: It says AI technology moves quickly, so expertise and mental models based on earlier capabilities can become outdated and mislead leaders.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I've seen this a lot, and I think it comes down to a few things.

The first is that the playbooks these leaders learned were often really good playbooks, but they were tuned for a different environment. If you grew up in, say, the SaaS era, you learned that you build a product, you find product-market fit, you hire a sales team, you scale go-to-market, and the technology mostly stays put while you do that. In AI companies right now, the technology under your feet is shifting every few months. A capability that was impossible six months ago is suddenly cheap. So the instinct to lock in a roadmap and execute for eighteen months, which was a virtue before, can actually be a liability. You have to be willing to throw away work, and a lot of experienced leaders find that psychologically very hard, because they were rewarded their whole careers for not doing that.

The second thing is speed of iteration. In AI, so much of the progress comes from trying things fast. Prototyping a new application used to take months, and now a small team can get something working in a few days. The leaders who do well are the ones who are willing to get their hands dirty, go look at the actual outputs, go look at the data, and make decisions in days rather than quarters. Some leaders coming from large, mature organizations have gotten used to operating through layers of people and process, and that layer of abstraction between them and the technology really slows them down.

And the third thing, honestly, is technical depth. I don't think every leader needs to be able to train a model, but I do think you need enough understanding to have good judgment about what's feasible, what's hard, and what's hype. When the ground is moving this fast, you can't fully outsource that judgment to your engineers, because the strategic decisions and the technical decisions are so tightly coupled. The leaders I see struggling are often the ones who say, "I'll handle the business side, and the technical people will handle the AI side." That separation worked when the technology was stable. It doesn't work very well now.

So I'd say it's less about these people being less capable, and more that the environment punishes certain habits that used to be rewarded. The ones who adapt are the ones who stay curious, keep learning, and are humble enough to realize that a lot of what they know needs to be relearned.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts leaders’ accustomed eighteen-month roadmaps and quarter-based decisions with AI companies’ need to adapt and iterate in days.

r002.rationale: It says established playbooks were tuned for a different environment and can become liabilities as AI technology shifts, requiring leaders to discard work and relearn.

astra-6.text:
I think one challenge is that success teaches you a set of instincts, and those instincts depend on the environment in which you learned them. If you’ve spent twenty years building software a certain way, you become very good at knowing how to organize a team, how to plan a product, how to allocate resources. But when the technology changes, some of those intuitions need to change as well.

For example, a leader might look at a product idea and assume it requires a large engineering team and a year of development. With AI, perhaps a small team can build something useful in a few weeks. But the reverse can happen, too: something that looks straightforward in a demo can be very difficult to make reliable enough for customers. So you need a different understanding of what’s easy, what’s hard, and where the uncertainty lies.

That doesn’t mean experience is less valuable. But I think you have to be willing to become a beginner again in some areas. Ask questions, work closely with the people building the technology, and test whether your old assumptions still hold. The difficulty is when past success gives you so much confidence that you stop doing that learning.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how AI changes leaders’ assumptions about what is easy or hard, but does not attribute their difficulty to a mismatch in operating pace.

r002.rationale: It says that when technology changes, some instincts built in the earlier environment need to change, and advises leaders to test whether their old assumptions still hold.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the challenges is that when you’ve been successful, you build up a set of instincts about how companies work. And those instincts may have been exactly right for the environment you were in. But when you move into an AI company, some of those assumptions need to be reexamined.

For example, how do you decide what’s feasible to build? How quickly should a team be able to ship something? What should you build yourself versus get from a vendor? With AI, the answers can change very quickly. So a playbook that served you well even a few years ago can lead you to make the wrong decisions today.

That doesn’t mean the leadership experience isn’t valuable. It’s very valuable. But I think you have to pair it with humility and a willingness to get into the details, learn from the technical team, and update your judgment. The danger is coming in and saying, ‘I’ve seen this before; I know how to scale it,’ when there are important parts of it that really are different.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that AI can change how quickly teams ship, but does not clearly say leaders struggle because their accustomed operating pace mismatches the pace AI companies require.

r002.rationale: It says AI changes answers quickly, so a playbook that worked a few years ago can lead to wrong decisions today.
